newsitem.title: USA: Possible Thai bailout has parallels with Mexico deal.
newsitem.headline: Possible Thai bailout has parallels with Mexico deal.

text.p: Thailand's decision to seek foreign help to rescue its shaky economy raises the prospect of a big international bail-out like that won two years ago by Mexico, but it is too early to say exactly what must be done.
An IMF spokesman, welcoming news that a loan package could be on the agenda, said on Tuesday that other countries would probably be involved with any future deal.

"The (Thai) authorities have made clear they are looking for an IMF support package," the spokesman said. "Obviously we welcome that news and will be discussing a package with them which will probably involve support both from us and from bilateral sources."

Japanese officials have indicated they would consider joining an IMF-backed package and economists said a Thailand deal involving states and international financial institutions would be similar to the Mexico one, but on a smaller scale.
"Mexico got $50 billion and the Thais need much less than that," said Bejoy Das Gupta, senior economist at the Institute for International Finance.
"What they need right now is a comprehensive economic programme, or at least for the IMF to come out and say that we are working with them to arrive at a comprehensive package."

Thai authorities had until this week insisted that they would not need IMF help to resolve their economic woes, which centre on a fragile financial system, a wide current account deficit and doubts about currency policy after the central bank was forced to allow the baht to float.

Analysts said government credibility had been dented by months of policy wavering. Commercial loans -- a possibility only a few months ago -- were no longer an option, so markets needed the reassurance of an IMF plan.
"Even three or four months ago they could have gone to the market and raised money there," said a Washington economist who visits Thailand regularly.
"But the policy delays and the vacuum over the last six months meant that they have lost credibility. At last they are coming round to the idea that they need the IMF."

Economists say Thailand will probably need between $10 billion and $20 billion, with IMF money bound to be linked to tough conditions on banking policy or monetary issues. Once the IMF has launched the loan bandwagon, others could follow.
An official with the World Bank, the IMF's sister organisation, said the issue was under discussion.
"Our role as a development institution is to look at long-term economic development...but we are examining this whole thing very closely right now and are reviewing our position," he said.

The IMF has already used fast-track regulations drawn up after the Mexico crisis to approve a $1.1 billion loan for the Philippines, which was forced to devalue the peso soon after the Thai baht crashed.
The money was approved just a week after the peso devaluation, helped by the fact that the Philippines already had a loan programme with the IMF.
Thailand, which has guarded its financial independence jealously, has not borrowed money from the IMF for more than a decade and it could take longer for a programme to be in place.
But analysts said the mere fact that the two sides were talking would be good for markets.

"Everybody has been hoping that Thailand would move in this direction," said Susan Levine, director with Emerging Markets Partnership, adding that an IMF-style programme geared at ensuring macroeconomic stability would have to be positive.
